shipped_rows.title_o: An intraindividual process approach to the relationship between extraversion and positive affect: Is acting extraverted as "good" as being extraverted?

blind_target.title: The causal effects of extraversion on positive affect and neuroticism on negative affect: Manipulating state extraversion and state neuroticism in an experimental approach.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Although possible, two studies have assessed negative affect under similar circumstances and have failed to find the state by trait interaction that would suggest a mood cost for acting counterdispositionally (McNiel & Fleeson, 2006; McNiel et al., 2010). Therefore, our studies include between-subjects manipulations, larger sample sizes, and measures of both positive and negative affect to better assess any possible distress that might accompany counterdispositional behavior.
blind_target.outcome_quote: This study tested whether the pattern of relationships among extraversion, mood, behavior, and cognition found in Study 1 would generalize to a new interview situation. Very similar to previous research, participants reported more positive affect when acting extraverted, and this did not depend on their dispositional levels of extraversion. We again tested whether acting counterdispositionally might cause negative affect (along with positive affect in the case of introverts) and again failed to find any evidence for this idea.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The reported positive-affect benefit and/or absence of dispositional negative-affect cost agrees with this original’s findings. Cognitive depletion is a novel extension, not a failed replication of these mood findings.

corrected_value.title: The causal effects of extraversion on positive affect and neuroticism on negative affect: Manipulating state extraversion and state neuroticism in an experimental approach
corrected_value.title_o: The causal effects of extraversion on positive affect and neuroticism on negative affect: Manipulating state extraversion and state neuroticism in an experimental approach
corrected_value.evidence_quote: Although possible, two studies have assessed negative affect under similar circumstances and have failed to find the state by trait interaction that would suggest a mood cost for acting counterdispositionally (McNiel & Fleeson, 2006; McNiel et al., 2010). On the other hand, one of these samples was small (n⫽45) and both employed a within-subject design that could promote demand or carryover effects. In fact, the studies did find significant order effects and some inconsistent trait and acting condition effects on negative affect. So although there was not a significant interaction suggesting an affective cost, the full mood consequences of acting more or less extraverted require some clarification, particularly with regard to negative affect. Therefore, our studies include between-subjects manipulations, larger sample sizes, and measures of both positive and negative affect to better assess any possible distress that might accompany counterdispositional behavior.
corrected_value.outcome_quote: Results replicated and extended past findings suggesting that acting extraverted produces hedonic benefits regardless of disposition. Positive affect increased and negative affect did not, even for participants acting out of character.

prior_decision.quote: Although possible, two studies have assessed negative affect under similar circumstances and have failed to find the state by trait interaction that would suggest a mood cost for acting counterdispositionally (McNiel & Fleeson, 2006; McNiel et al., 2010). On the other hand, one of these samples was small (n⫽45) and both employed a within-subject design that could promote demand or carryover effects. In fact, the studies did find significant order effects and some inconsistent trait and acting condition effects on negative affect. So although there was not a significant interaction suggesting an affective cost, the full mood consequences of acting more or less extraverted require some clarification, particularly with regard to negative affect. Therefore, our studies include between-subjects manipulations, larger sample sizes, and measures of both positive and negative affect to better assess any possible distress that might accompany counterdispositional behavior.
prior_decision.reason: The paper directly re-tests McNiel and Fleeson's (2006) empirical finding that manipulating state extraversion/introversion produces no state-by-trait interaction on negative affect (and increases positive affect regardless of disposition), explicitly critiquing the small sample size and within-subject design of the two prior negative-affect studies and conducting a stronger between-subjects test across Studies 1 and 2 that confirms the absence of a counterdispositional negative-affect cost (successful replication).
